title: Numbers That Follow Each Other

concept.title: Walk from 1 to the last number, and stay close enough to the next given number
body: A number path puzzle is an `n` by `n` grid in which the numbers `1 .. n*n` must be written once each so that **each number is next to the following number** (above, below, left or right). So the numbers form a walk through all the cells. Some numbers are given, among them always 1 and `n*n`. The empty cells (`0`) must be filled. Count the ways to complete the grid.

Walk the path from 1: the cell of the number `v + 1` is one of the 4 neighbours of the cell of `v`. If `v + 1` is **given**, its cell is fixed and it must be a neighbour; otherwise try every free neighbour that is empty and not used. A free cell must not be a cell of some given number (that number has to stand there).

The last check is the important **pruning**: if the next given number `g` is at Manhattan distance `d` from the new cell, it needs at least `d` steps, so we must have `d <= g - (v + 1)`. Without this test the search wanders far away from the numbers it must reach and wastes a huge amount of time.

statement: An `n` by `n` grid contains some of the numbers 1 to `n * n` (different numbers) and zeros for empty cells. The numbers 1 and `n * n` are always given. Fill the empty cells with the missing numbers so that every number from 1 to `n * n - 1` is in a cell next to the cell of the following number (neighbours share a side). Count the ways to fill the grid.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has `n` integers.
outputFormat: Print the number of completions (it can be 0).
constraints: The nonzero numbers are different, and the numbers 1 and n * n are among them.

examples.note: The number 2 must be next to 1, and the only free cell next to 1 is on its right; then 3 goes below 2, and 4 is next to 3. The grid becomes 1 2 / 4 3: one way.

hints: Start at the cell of 1 and place the numbers in order.
If the next number is given, check that its cell is a neighbour; otherwise try the empty unused neighbours.
Stop a branch when the next given number is too far away to be reached in the steps that are left.

The cell of `v + 1` is a neighbour of the cell of `v`: if `v + 1` is given, its cell must be that neighbour; otherwise any empty unused neighbour that is close enough to the next given number is tried, and the cell is marked and unmarked around the recursive call.
solution.complexity: Time exponential in the empty cells, small thanks to the distance test; space O(n^2).
